## Required reading

::: {.lectura}
Noble, W. S. (2017). [Ten simple rules for writing a response to reviewers](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005730). *PLOS Computational Biology*, 13(10), e1005730.
:::

## 1. Cover letters

A cover letter to an editor is short (one page) and answers three questions: **what** you are submitting, **why** it matters to this journal's readers, and **formal statements** (originality, no simultaneous submission, conflicts of interest, data availability). Do not repeat the abstract.

> Dear Dr Smith,
>
> Please find attached our manuscript "Supervision quality predicts doctoral completion: a five-year cohort study", which we submit for consideration as a Research Article in *Higher Education*.
>
> Most studies of doctoral attrition are cross-sectional. Following 1,200 students for five years, we show that changes in supervision quality predict completion better than funding. These findings will interest readers working on doctoral education policy.
>
> The manuscript has not been published or submitted elsewhere. All authors approved it and declare no conflicts of interest. Data and code are available at [DOI].
>
> Yours sincerely,

## 2. Writing a review

A useful review has a clear structure: a **summary** of the paper's claims (to show you understood them), the **main concerns** (validity, methods, interpretation), **minor points**, and, if the journal asks, a recommendation. Be specific ("the model does not control for cohort; please add it or explain why not") and kind: criticise the work, not the authors. Avoid asking for a different paper.

## 3. Responding to reviewers

Noble (2017) offers rules that turn a stressful task into a manageable one. The most important:

- **Provide an overview**, then respond to **every point**, quoting each comment in full.
- **Be polite and respectful** to all reviewers, even when they are wrong.
- **Accept the blame** when the reviewer misunderstood: it usually means the text was unclear, so clarify it.
- **Make the response self-contained**: the editor should not need to search the manuscript; quote the changed text.
- **Respond to the reviewer's intent**, not only the literal request.
- **Be clear about what changed**, with page and line numbers.
- When you disagree, give **evidence and reasons**, and consider doing the requested analysis anyway (perhaps in the supplement).

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| *The reviewer is wrong.* | *We respectfully disagree, because…* |
| *This was already explained.* | *We have clarified this point in the Methods (p. 6, lines 120-128).* |
| *We do not have time to do this.* | *This analysis is beyond the scope of this study, but we now mention it as a limitation (p. 15).* |

## 4. Academic emails

Short, with a clear subject line and the request in the first two sentences. Formal openings (*Dear Professor García,*), a polite request (*Would you be able to…? I would be grateful if…*) and a closing (*Best regards, / Kind regards,*). Avoid Spanish calques such as *I write you to…* (→ *I am writing to…*) and *Waiting for your answer* (→ *I look forward to hearing from you*).

## Activities

::: {.clasificar #ia-e5-tone titulo="Appropriate tone for a response to reviewers?" categorias="Appropriate|Inappropriate"}
- "We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment and have added the analysis (p. 9)." → Appropriate
- "The reviewer clearly did not read the paper carefully." → Inappropriate
- "We respectfully disagree: as shown in Table 3, the effect remains after adjustment." → Appropriate
- "This is obvious and does not need explanation." → Inappropriate
:::

::: {.ordenar #ia-e5-response titulo="Order a response to a reviewer's comment"}
1. Quote the reviewer's comment in full
2. Thank the reviewer or acknowledge the point
3. Explain what you did or why you disagree
4. Show the changed text with page and line numbers
:::

::: {.escenario #ia-e5-escenario titulo="A difficult reviewer"}
Reviewer 2 says your sample is too small and asks you to collect more data, which would take a year.

### The comment {#e5e-inicio}
How do you respond?

- ["The sample is adequate. We will not collect more data."](#e5e-rechazo)
- [Acknowledge the concern and report a power analysis and confidence intervals](#e5e-evidencia)

### Dismissive {#e5e-rechazo .final .mal}
A refusal without evidence will probably lead to rejection and does not address the reviewer's intent: they are worried about precision.

### Evidence {#e5e-evidencia}
The analysis shows that small effects cannot be ruled out. What do you add?

- [Nothing more: the analysis is enough](#e5e-nada)
- [A clear limitation in the Methods and more cautious conclusions](#e5e-limitacion)

### Partial {#e5e-nada .final .regular}
Better, but the text still claims more than the data support.

### Complete response {#e5e-limitacion .final .bien}
You respond to the intent (precision), report evidence, state the limitation within the methodology and calibrate the conclusions (chapter 3). The editor can now judge the paper fairly.
:::

## Assignment {#reto-e5}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Challenge for chapter 5 · The full cycle
1. Write a cover letter for one of your manuscripts (or a fictitious one).
2. Write a one-page peer review of a published preprint in your field.
3. Using a real or invented set of three reviewer comments, write a complete response letter following Noble (2017).

**Submission:** use the [assignment template](plantillas/entrega_reto.qmd). This challenge **has no solution in the book**.
:::

{{< longmcq "Ignore the comment" "*Explain respectfully with evidence and reasons" "Complain to the editor" >}}
:::

::: {.webex-solution boton="Show explanations"}
- What, why this journal, formal statements.
- Quote each comment in full.
- Accept the blame and clarify.
- "I am writing to ask…"
- Specific and kind.
- The editor should not have to search.
- A common calque from Spanish.
- "We respectfully disagree, because…"
:::
